analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover childhood vaccines with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal health insurance law to require group health plans and individual health insurance policies to cover all routine childhood immunizations for dependents under 19, following the CDC's recommended vaccine schedule, with no deductibles, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing. It also would have covered vaccines bought in the individual market the same way. It was referred to two House committees and two subcommittees, none of which acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with insured children under 19. Routine childhood shots would be covered in full — no deductible, coinsurance, or copay — including the cost of the vaccine itself, so parents would no longer face out-of-pocket charges for well-child vaccinations.

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans and health insurance issuers must cover routine immunizations for every dependent under 19, with no deductibles, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing, following the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices' recommended childhood schedule, including the vaccine itself.
The same coverage requirement applies to health insurance sold in the individual market, so families buying their own coverage get the same protection as those with job-based plans.
The requirements apply to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2004, with a phase-in for plans governed by pre-existing collective bargaining agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and policyholders who fund health plans would bear the cost of covering vaccines without cost-sharing, which would flow into premiums. Self-insured employer plans would have to add the benefit directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises plan costs: covering vaccines in full, including the vaccine itself, means insurers and self-insured employers absorb those costs, which are typically passed on through higher premiums for all enrollees.
The bill reaches only people who have health insurance. Uninsured children would get no new coverage from this bill; separate public programs, not this mandate, serve that population.
A federal mandate sets one nationwide benefit floor regardless of state-by-state choices about what insurance must cover, overriding state benefit mandates with the federal standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: eliminating out-of-pocket charges for childhood vaccines removes a known barrier to timely immunization for insured families. The cost is a modest premium increase spread across all enrollees. It does nothing for uninsured children, the group with the biggest immunization gaps.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce committees, sent to their health and employer-employee subcommittees, and never moved again; no committee or subcommittee vote, no House floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Gene Green introduced the bill on May 14, 2003, with 14 original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On June 11, 2003, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on June 20, 2003, to the Education and the Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
No further action appears in the record: neither committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors are better off because the bill died: they never had to add first-dollar vaccine coverage or absorb the cost. Families with insured children continue to face whatever cost-sharing their plans apply to shots.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered introductory remarks.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to its Health Subcommittee, which never acted; the committee never reported the bill.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, which never acted; the committee never reported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly all Democratic — 13 of the 14 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican — and no committee or floor votes were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers in both group and individual markets to cover childhood vaccines with no cost-sharing, raising their benefit costs. Defeating the bill preserved their discretion over benefit design and cost-sharing.
Self-insured employer plans would have had to add the first-dollar vaccine benefit, a new plan cost, though a modest one spread across enrollees.

Removing cost-sharing makes it easier for families to get children vaccinated on schedule, supporting demand for vaccines and vaccination visits. Neither the sources nor the record shows them taking a position on the bill.
